newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan Islamists say might review election boycott.
newsitem.headline: Jordan Islamists say might review election boycott.

text.p: Jordan's powerful Moslem Brotherhood said on Tuesday it might abandon a boycott of parliamentary elections if the government responded favourably to its grievances.
Brotherhood leader Abdul Majeed al-Thuneibat met Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali on Tuesday, for the first time since his group's July decision to boycott the November elections.
The group called the action to protest at government policies they say curb public freedoms.
"We hope this dialogue will lead to positive results...and allow us to go back on our boycott decision to one of participation," Thuneibat told reporters.
"If the causes that led to the decision are gone or some of them and it was convincing to us, then we will retreat from the boycott," he said.

The meeting with Majali focused on how to launch a long-delayed dialogue on the boycott call, which has plunged the country into political turmoil, he said, but added that no date had been agreed for this to start.

The Islamist movement, which commands wide grassroots support, demands that the government revoke interim controls on the press and the economy ordered during the parliamentary recess. They movement says the limits are unconstitutional.
The Islamist boycott poses the first serious setback to Jordan's restored parliamentary life since King Hussein launched cautious steps towards political liberalisation in 1989.

The smaller secular opposition and prominent independent figures have also heeded the Islamists' call, adding to the government's worries as it gears to the first elections since Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
King Hussein insisted on Monday that the elections would take place on time, with or without the participation of the Islamists, but he left the door open for dialogue.
Independent observers have said that if the polls went ahead without them might mean a lack of a credible parliamentary opposition, tarnishing liberal Jordan's image in the Arab world.
